reports.name: Pete Crow-Armstrong
reports.published_report: The xwOBA and xSLG both land in the 80th percentile, but the chase rate sits at 34.9%, bottom fifth of the league, and that gap is the whole argument about what Crow-Armstrong is. He draws an 11.8% walk rate while chasing more than a third of pitches outside the zone, which means he's doing damage on contact rather than taking pitches, and the 25.9% strikeout rate reflects what happens when that approach meets a pitcher willing to exploit it. A .272/.361/.496 line with 31 home runs and 38 stolen bases in 692 plate appearances is a legitimate star season if the walk rate holds; if pitchers find the discipline hole and the walks dry up, you're left with the power and the sprint speed at the 96th percentile, which still profiles as a useful regular. The stolen base volume is the one piece that doesn't depend on anything.

reports.name: Shohei Ohtani
reports.published_report: A .408 xwOBA at the plate and a 2.72 xERA on the mound: the tension in this profile isn't whether he's elite, it's whether he's actually doing both simultaneously as a full-time DH who pitches. The batting Statcast card is essentially a pure contact-and-power argument: 16.9% barrel rate, 14.3% walk rate, a 23.1% strikeout rate that sits near league average despite a 29.9% whiff rate, which means his plate discipline is doing real work to keep the strikeouts manageable. On the mound, a 2.72 xERA paired with 30.4% whiff rate and a barrel rate allowed of just 3.8% says the stuff translates to genuine run prevention, with a 7.6% walk rate as the one place opposing offenses can find oxygen. The projection, .282/.391/.542 with 38 home runs across 690 plate appearances, lives or dies on his arm staying healthy enough to give us the pitcher half of this, because without it we're pricing a very good DH, not the most valuable two-way asset in the sport.

reports.name: Cam Schlittler

reports.published_report: The xBA sitting at .300, 98th percentile, while average exit velocity checks in at 87.5 mph tells you almost everything about how Peña works: he makes contact everywhere, places it well, and gets more out of weak-to-medium contact than most hitters alive. The projection's .280 AVG, .340 OBP, 16 home runs, and 15 stolen bases in 482 plate appearances is the logical translation of that profile, a shortstop who contributes across the board without dominating any single category. The whole thing hinges on contact quality staying cheap, because a 4.7% barrel rate and 38.4% hard-hit rate mean there's no exit-velo floor to catch him if the placement degrades, and if pitchers find a way to make his 33.8% chase rate punish him more, the .280 average erodes and the rest of the line thins with it. What you get when it holds is a genuine everyday shortstop, not a star, but a player who earns every plate appearance.

reports.name: Sandy Alcantara
reports.published_report: The case for Alcantara rests almost entirely on contact suppression, and the current Statcast profile makes that case cleanly. A 5.3% barrel rate and 34.5% hard-hit rate say hitters are getting to his pitches but not doing much with them, which is exactly what you'd expect from a 97.5 mph fastball that generates weak contact rather than empty swings — his 21.8% whiff rate sits in the bottom quarter of the league, so he's pitching to contact on purpose. The control holds it together: a 6.5% walk rate ranks in the 80th percentile, meaning he can live in the zone without the barrel rate climbing on him. The projection landing at 207.6 innings with a 3.99 ERA reflects a healthy workhorse rebuilding from Tommy John, and if the strikeouts stay near his current 18.8%, he's a back-to-front innings-eater rather than a true ace, but that's 21 quality starts worth of value regardless.

reports.name: Zack Gelof
reports.published_report: The Statcast profile has one loud number and one quiet one, and together they tell you what he is. His 23.9% chase rate sits in the 84th percentile, meaning he genuinely won't expand the zone, but a 5.7% walk rate that ranks in the 14th percentile says pitchers have figured out they can work him carefully without much punishment, and the .289 xwOBA is the result. The projection's .772 OPS across 404 plate appearances feels like an honest ceiling given that the expected slugging sits at .375 despite the speed, 28.8 ft/s, doing real work on the bases. He's a second-division regular if the walk rate stays buried; the whole profile upgrades if he learns to convert that chase discipline into actual damage counts.

reports.name: Taj Bradley
reports.published_report: The strikeouts and the contact quality are pulling in opposite directions. Bradley's 27.2 K% sits in the 79th percentile, but hitters are barreling him at 9.8% and making hard contact 45.3% of the time, numbers that rank near the bottom of the league. The fastball at 96.9 mph generates swings and misses, yet his 29.2 Chase% tells you he's not expanding the zone to manufacture the outs, meaning the whiffs come in the zone where hard contact lives too. If he sharpens his command, that 9.4 BB% is the anchor dragging the profile, he becomes a mid-rotation arm who earns his 191 projected strikeouts; if the contact rates don't soften, that 3.91 xERA starts feeling generous.

reports.name: Sam Antonacci
reports.published_report: The contact grades are the story here, and they don't match the rest of the profile. A 15.5% whiff rate and 22.8% chase rate put Antonacci among the better bat-to-ball outfielders in the league, and that's what drives the .289 xBA. The problem is that 87.5 mph average exit velocity and a 36.2% hard-hit rate sit near the bottom of the league in raw power, so the xSLG of .426 is getting built almost entirely on placement and contact shape rather than authority. The projection's .275/.366/.403 line holds together if he stays this disciplined and keeps finding gaps, but a 7.4% walk rate means the plate approach is less patient than it looks — he's earning his .366 OBP by making contact, not drawing free passes, and any drift in bat-to-ball quality collapses the profile fast. This reads as a legitimate second-division regular, maybe an everyday player if the hit tool keeps translating; without the contact grades, there's a 21-steal, no-power outfielder with a middling OBP and not much else.

reports.name: Ryan Weathers
reports.published_report: The strikeout and walk numbers are genuinely good. Weathers sits at 26.6% K% and 6.7% BB%, both landing in the upper quarter of the league, and a 27.9% whiff rate backs the swing-and-miss. The problem is everything that makes contact: a 10.2% barrel rate and 42.3% hard-hit rate that land near the bottom of the league suggest the stuff doesn't miss barrels the way it misses bats, and a 4.56 xERA is the game being honest about what that combination produces. The ValuCast projection at 4.16 ERA over 147.4 innings reflects a pitcher who can churn through a rotation spot without embarrassing himself, and 162 strikeouts over that workload carry weight, but the profile hinges entirely on whether he can suppress damage on contact — if that barrel rate doesn't come down, the strikeouts become window dressing on a back-end arm.

reports.name: Reid Detmers
reports.published_report: The xERA sits at 3.26 while the projection ERA is 4.05, and that gap is the whole Detmers argument. His Statcast contact profile is legitimately clean, a 27.4% strikeout rate with a .281 xwOBA, but his 94.1 mph fastball generates bottom-third spin at 2154 rpm, which is exactly the kind of thing that makes sequencing and location load-bearing. When he's locating, the whiff rate holds and hitters don't elevate; when he isn't, that fastball gets found, and the ERA drifts back toward his surface numbers. If the command holds across a full 177.3 innings, you have a mid-rotation arm punching above his stuff; if it slips, the strikeouts stay but the ERA settles right where the projection has it.

reports.published_report: The fastball sits at 96.9 mph with 2326 rpm of spin, which is a legitimate weapon, and the 6.1% barrel rate shows he's keeping the hardest contact off the barrel. The problem is that 45.4% hard-hit rate, a number that sits near the bottom of the league, and a 22.2% whiff rate that doesn't give him a reliable escape hatch when he does get hit. His xERA of 3.91 is meaningfully better than the projected 4.50 ERA, which means strand rate and sequencing are working against him as much as the underlying contact profile is. If the stuff commands well enough to suppress barrels and the hard-hit rate pulls back, he's a mid-rotation piece turning in quality starts; if the hard-hit rate holds where it is, the 4.50 is the floor and a 22.9% strikeout rate won't bail him out.

reports.name: Nelson Rada
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 383 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The contact-and-run profile here is legitimate, but the power ceiling is where the conversation ends. At AAA in 2026, Rada is hitting .288/.391/.367 across 383 plate appearances, with 29 stolen bases, 50 walks, and only 58 strikeouts. That translates to a K% that would sit below league average in the majors and a walk rate above it, a genuinely unusual combination at 20 years old. The problem is the .08 ISO at AAA, which translates to .093 in MLB context — most everyday hitters are well above that, and the profile hinges entirely on whether the speed and on-base skills carry enough value without it. If they do, he's a legitimate bench piece or platoon option; if the bat doesn't develop any pop as he ages, this is a depth profile that wears out its welcome quickly.

reports.name: Edward Cabrera
reports.published_report: The fastball sits 96.1 mph, and hitters chase his stuff at a 32.6% rate, so why is the xERA 4.87? That's the tension: loud raw stuff, brutal contact allowed when hitters do connect, with a barrel rate of 11.8% that ranks near the bottom of the league. The whiff rate is 26.4%, but a 9.4% walk rate bleeds away everything the chase numbers build, and the .338 xwOBA confirms the damage is repeated and structural. If the walks tighten and he stops living in the barrel zone, there's a back-end starter in there across a projected 114.6 innings; if they don't, he's a guy with a fastball and a ceiling he can't reach.

report_llm.text: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it's also the thing that makes it complicated. Fifty-seven walks against 83 strikeouts across 343 A-ball plate appearances in 2026, at age 19, gives Parker a 17% walk rate that translates to roughly 11.3% at the MLB level, meaningfully ahead of what most big-league hitters draw. The ISO that looks promising at A (.185) melts to .125 in translation, below the MLB average, and the profile hinges almost entirely on whether the discipline is portable: if the zone command travels and the gap power firms up, he's a second-division regular with a real OBP skill; if the power doesn't develop and advanced arms exploit the contact issues, the 21 stolen bases and the walks leave him a bench piece.

reports.name: Blake Mitchell
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 355 A+ PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is almost too good to be true for a 21-year-old catcher, and the strikeout rate is almost too bad to ignore. Mitchell has drawn 83 walks against 121 strikeouts at A+, a 23% walk rate that sits at the 99th percentile of the hitter pool while a 34% strikeout rate lands at the 8th. The .244 ISO and 18 stolen bases say the physical tools are present, but when A+ punch-outs translate to a 35.2% MLB-equivalent strikeout rate, the .16 MLB-equivalent ISO barely clears what the average big-leaguer posts, and the offensive identity becomes a walk-or-bust proposition. If the contact rate tightens even modestly, there's an everyday catching profile worth watching; if it doesn't, what's left is a bench bat with a good eye.

reports.name: Will Sanders
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is mixed over 48.3 AAA IP.
reports.published_report: The profile is functional, not loud. Across AAA & A+ this season, Sanders has a 3.7 ERA and 1.3 WHIP in 56 innings, and the walk rate is the thing to watch: 22 walks in that span, with a BB/9 that translates to 3.5 at the MLB level while the MLB average sits at 3.2. The strikeout number doesn't carry the load you'd want from a ceiling arm, 58 punchouts in those 56 innings translating to an 8.3 K/9, just below the MLB mean of 8.6. Everything here points to a depth arm, floor and ceiling both, and the path to something more hinges entirely on whether the command tightens enough to let the bat-missing play up. If it doesn't, you've got an organizational piece who eats innings without getting hitters out.

reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 81.7 AA IP.
reports.published_report: The translation is the problem. Across 81.7 innings at AA, Hartle is walking 3.6 per nine and striking out 8.3, and when those rates move to an MLB context, the strikeout rate falls to 7.5 while the league sits at 8.6, and the walk rate actually climbs to 3.7. The K-BB% translates to 10.3%, well short of the 13.5% MLB average, and that gap is where the profile gets honest about its ceiling. The walk control reads well enough at AA, a 71st-percentile mark in the pitcher pool, but if that control edge doesn't survive a major-league zone, there's no strikeout rate to carry him, and you're left with a depth arm, which is both the floor and the ceiling here.

reports.name: Jim Jarvis
reports.peak_summary: Projection: bench or platoon bat with low risk. The current bat shape is balanced over 348 AAA PA.
reports.published_report:
The contact-first shortstop profile is the whole argument here, and the power is what keeps the ceiling in check. Jim Jarvis is hitting .313 at AAA with 46 walks against 55 strikeouts in 348 plate appearances, and the MLB-equivalent translation puts his strikeout rate at 18.9% in a league that runs 22.0%, his walk rate at 10.8% where the field sits at 8.5%. The 32 stolen bases are loud. But six home runs and a .148 ISO at AAA translate to .13 against MLB pitching, and nothing in the shape of this profile suggests that gap narrows.

If the bat-to-ball and speed carry over, he's a low-end everyday shortstop; if a big league defense solves him, he's a reserve.
reports.report: Everyday contact regular, with a useful reserve floor; he consistently finishes at-bats with contact. The open question is damage against better pitching; the sample covers 348 PA in Triple-A, so confidence is high.

reports.name: Aidan Miller
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with high risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 489 AA PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the loudest thing in this profile, and it might also be its ceiling. At AA in 489 plate appearances, Miller posted a 15 BB% against a 24 K%, which translates across AAA & AA to a 12.3 BB% while the average MLB hitter draws 8.5%, and the ISO equivalent lands at .135, below the MLB mean of .150. The plate discipline is genuine and consistent; the power hasn't followed it there. If the ISO closes that gap as he moves up, he's a useful bench bat with real on-base value; if it stays where it translated, he's org depth who walks a lot without enough damage to matter at the position.

reports.name: Josh Stephan
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 91 AAA IP.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is doing real work here, and almost nothing else is. Stephan has issued 27 walks in 91 AAA innings this season, and that command translates cleanly to MLB — but the strikeout rate translates to 8.1 K/9 when most big-league rotations want more than that, and a 5.6 ERA sitting in the 30th percentile of his pool tells you the efficiency isn't masking a contact problem so much as coexisting with one. The whole profile hinges on whether the control holds up against a better class of hitter, because if it slips, there's no swing-and-miss ceiling to absorb the damage. Depth arm, ceiling and floor both.

reports.name: Drew Beam
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 83 AA IP.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the one thing working in his favor, and it's not enough. Drew Beam has held a 3.0 BB/9 at AA across 83 innings, which translates to 3.3 at the MLB level, essentially a wash against a sport where the average sits around that same number, but his strikeout rate tells the harder truth: 7.2 K/9 at AA becomes 6.9 in equivalent terms, well short of the MLB average 8.6. The 6.00 ERA over 17 starts is the outcome you'd expect when a pitcher can't miss bats consistently, and the whole profile hinges on whether his command tightens enough to compensate for limited swing-and-miss. If it doesn't, the ceiling and floor are the same place: a depth arm who fills a rotation spot in a pinch without holding it.

reports.name: Luis Perales
reports.peak_summary: Projection: depth arm with medium risk. The current pitching shape is starter volume over 73.7 AAA IP.
reports.published_report:
The ERA looks good. The walk rate says don't trust it.

At AAA in 2026, Perales carries a 3.7 ERA and 1.3 WHIP across 73.7 innings, and those surface numbers have real appeal, but he's issued 40 walks while striking out 66, and when you translate that to an MLB context, the walk rate blooms to 4.4 per nine while MLB hitters average just 3.2 allowed. His K-BB% translates to 9.4% against a field sitting at 13.5%, and that gap is the whole tension here: the run suppression is holding at AAA but the command profile is the kind that unravels fast when the level gets harder to fool. If the walks tighten, there's a back-of-rotation arm somewhere in this profile; if they don't, the ceiling and floor converge at organizational depth.

reports.name: Lucas Gordon

reports.published_report: The walk rate is the argument here, and it doesn't make one. Across 92 innings at AA, Lucas Gordon has issued 42 walks against 101 strikeouts, and the MLB translation puts his BB/9 at 4.1 while his strikeout rate actually softens to 8.3, both figures landing below where an average MLB starter sits. The 1.3 WHIP looks survivable until you remember the ERA sits at 5.1, which is what tends to happen when you're throwing free bases at a rate that doesn't improve on translation. reports.name: Tsung-Che Cheng
reports.peak_summary: Projection: organizational depth with medium risk. The current bat shape is mixed over 240 AAA PA.
reports.published_report: The walk rate is the honest edge here. Thirty-two walks in 240 AAA plate appearances translates to a 10.5% walk rate against an MLB average of 8.5%, which is a real skill and the thing that keeps his profile from being merely a glove-and-speed placeholder. The speed is loud too, 10 stolen bases already this season, and the .351 OBP at AAA reflects both. Where it gets complicated is the power: a .17 ISO at AAA softens to .142 in MLB equivalent terms, right at or just below league average, which means the offensive profile leans heavily on getting on base rather than doing damage once he does. If the walk rate travels and the contact holds, 60 strikeouts in 240 PA is a tick above comfortable at the big-league level, Cheng is a viable bench bat who can play shortstop and run; if the strikeout rate creeps and the ISO doesn't grow, the floor is organizational depth.
reports.report: The sample covers 240 PA in Triple-A, so confidence is high. He forces pitchers into the zone and takes the free pass. The line does not show a second offensive strength at the same level. The walks create an everyday path, but the present outcome is a reserve.
